conversations.title: I am launching a new B2B analytics app next mont

messages.content: I am launching a new B2B analytics app next month with a team of 3. Give me a simple 3-step launch plan.

Here is a simple, three-step plan built for a three-person team with a launch date next month.

1. Finalize the product and your story
Spend the first two weeks locking down what you are actually selling. Pick one ideal customer profile and the single problem you solve better than anyone else. Freeze your launch feature set and cut anything that is not demo-ready or bug-free. Write a short, jargon-free pitch and a ten-minute demo script that shows a clear before-and-after. Set up a simple landing page with a Calendly link so interested buyers can book a conversation the moment they hear about you.

2. Fill your pipeline with warm conversations
In week three, make a list of twenty to thirty target companies that fit your profile, starting with people in your founders’ extended networks. Send personalized, low-pressure outreach that references something specific about their business rather than a generic blast. Offer early access or a founding-customer discount in exchange for honest feedback and a potential testimonial. Your goal before launch day is five to eight qualified demo conversations on the calendar.

3. Launch week and first wins
Do a soft launch to your waitlist and network first, then open to the broader market. With only three people, you are the sales, support, and product team, so run every demo yourself. After each conversation, ask one question: what would make this a must-buy? Use those answers to fix friction immediately. Close the week by converting one to three design partners or paying pilots, then set a thirty-day goal for the next batch of customers.

If you want, I can help you draft the outreach messages, the demo script, or a simple launch-week checklist.
For step 1, how should our 3-person team decide between a free trial and a freemium plan?

This is one of those early choices that shapes everything downstream, so it’s worth pausing on. For a three-person B2B analytics team, the decision really comes down to three questions: who your buyer is, how complex your product is, and how much support you can personally handle.

A free trial gives someone a fully-featured sandbox for a set period—usually 14 or 30 days. It works well when your ideal customer is a technical decision-maker who can self-serve, when your product requires a bit of setup to see value, and when you want to filter for teams that are genuinely ready to buy. The downside is that trials can feel high-pressure, and if your onboarding isn’t frictionless, you’ll lose people who just wanted to poke around.

Freemium offers a permanently free tier with limited features. It’s great for driving top-of-funnel awareness, for products where users can get meaningful value quickly, and for building a community or data network. But in B2B, freemium can also attract a lot of low-intent users, dilute your support capacity, and make it harder to justify a paid upgrade unless your free tier is deliberately constrained.

For a small analytics team launching next month, I’d lean toward a free trial unless you have a specific reason to do freemium. Here’s a quick way to decide:

1. Can a prospect see a clear “aha” moment in under 10 minutes of signing up? If yes, freemium might work. If they need to connect a data source, build a dashboard, or wait for results, a trial is more honest.
2. Is your sales cycle short enough that a 2-week trial fits inside it? If you’re expecting a conversation within a week, a trial gives you a natural checkpoint. If your buyers take months to evaluate, a trial might expire before they even talk to you.
3. How much live support can you give? With three people, every support ticket is a distraction from building the product. Trials tend to generate fewer “what does this button do” questions because users are actively evaluating. Freemium can quietly accumulate a long tail of free users who never convert.

If you’re still torn, a hybrid often works best: offer a free trial, but let users who want to keep exploring after the trial expires downgrade to a limited freemium view. That way you don’t lose the relationship entirely, and you keep the door open without burning your support hours.

Want to walk through your specific buyer persona together? That usually makes the choice obvious within ten minutes.
What are the biggest customer concerns in our Pricing Analysis simulation?

Based on the simulated persona responses in "Clamir Studio Pro — Usage vs. Seat Pricing Analysis":

1. Step-Up Gap ($0 to $149/mo): Value Optimizers (69/100 acceptance) noted that jumping directly from a $0 Explorer plan to $149/month feels steep for solo founders running 5–8 studies a month.
2. Deliverable Verification: Prospective buyers want to inspect at least one sample full-fidelity PDF export on the free tier before committing to a recurring subscription.
3. Quota Clarity: Personas recommended replacing "Limited AI agent usage" with an explicit monthly query number (e.g., 25 AI Agent queries/month).

Note: These insights reflect simulated AI persona evaluations, not actual human survey respondents.
